body:
## Problem

The public, unauthenticated /api/github/open-pull-requests endpoint accepts a refresh=true query parameter that unconditionally bypasses the in-memory cache and re-triggers the full expensive GitHub GraphQL crawl (see the N+1 finding), with no authentication, rate limiting, or per-caller throttling anywhere in front of it.

## Evidence

Program.cs line 57 registers the endpoint with no auth requirement: app.MapGet("/api/github/open-pull-requests", GetOpenPullRequestsAsync) -- no .RequireAuthorization(). Line 101 passes the raw flag straight through: await reports.GetOpenPullRequestsAsync(owner, refresh == true, cancellationToken). PullRequestReportService.cs line 39 honors it unconditionally: if (!refresh && _cache.TryGetValue(cacheKey, out ...)).

## Impact

Any anonymous caller can repeatedly call GET /api/github/open-pull-requests?refresh=true (optionally varying owner=, which is also honored, to target arbitrary GitHub accounts) to force the server to burn its own configured GitHub token's GraphQL rate-limit budget on demand. Combined with the N+1 cost per call, a handful of requests can exhaust the token's hourly quota, breaking the service for legitimate use, while piling up long-running concurrent server-side requests.

## Fix

Require authentication/authorization (or at minimum an API key) for the refresh=true path, and/or apply ASP.NET Core's rate-limiting middleware to the endpoint -- especially for cache-bypassing requests -- so an anonymous caller cannot force unbounded upstream GitHub calls at will.

## Resolution
Added ASP.NET Core rate limiting (fixed-window, 10 req/min) on /api/github/open-pull-requests via .RequireRateLimiting(), returning 429 over the limit. Program.cs.
title: Unauthenticated refresh=true bypasses cache, enabling trivial GitHub-quota-exhaustion DoS

body:
## Problem

The `.Validate(...)` chain configured on `GitHubOptions` is never followed by `.ValidateOnStart()`, so .NET's Options validation only runs the first time `IOptionsMonitor<GitHubOptions>.CurrentValue` is accessed at request time -- not at application startup.

## Evidence

Program.cs lines 15-22:
builder.Services
    .AddOptions<GitHubOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection(GitHubOptions.SectionName))
    .Validate(options => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(options.Owner), "GitHub:Owner is required.")
    .Validate(options => options.CacheTtlSeconds is >= 0 and <= 86_400, "...")
    .Validate(options => options.RepositoryLimit is >= 1 and <= 1_000, "...")
    .Validate(options => options.PullRequestLimitPerRepository is >= 1 and <= 100, "...")
    .Validate(options => options.StatusCheckLimitPerPullRequest is >= 1 and <= 100, "...");
No `.ValidateOnStart()` terminates the chain.

## Impact

A container deployed with e.g. GitHub__RepositoryLimit=0 or GitHub__CacheTtlSeconds=-1 starts up successfully and passes /health/live and /health/ready (readiness only checks the token, see separate finding). It only throws Microsoft.Extensions.Options.OptionsValidationException the first time a real request reaches PullRequestReportService and touches _options.CurrentValue. That exception is not GitHubQueryException, so per a separate finding it also isn't caught by the endpoint -- the operator finds out from a runtime 500, not a failed deployment.

## Fix

Append `.ValidateOnStart()` to the options chain in Program.cs so misconfiguration fails fast during app.Build()/host startup instead of on first request.

## Resolution
Appended .ValidateOnStart() to the GitHubOptions builder chain in Program.cs; misconfiguration now fails at host startup instead of on first request.
title: GitHubOptions validation runs lazily, not at startup (.ValidateOnStart() missing)
Sequential per-PR GraphQL round-trip (N+1) for status details

body:
## Problem

GetOpenPullRequestsAsync's try/catch only handles GitHubQueryException. No global exception-handling middleware (UseExceptionHandler / IExceptionHandler) is registered anywhere in Program.cs.

## Evidence

Program.cs lines 99-121, the full try/catch block catches only `catch (GitHubQueryException)`. No `app.UseExceptionHandler(...)` call exists anywhere in the file.

## Impact

Any exception other than GitHubQueryException -- OptionsValidationException, a JsonException from an unexpected GraphQL response shape, an HttpRequestException from a connection failure, a cache exception -- propagates unhandled to ASP.NET Core's default handling, returning a bare contentless 500 instead of the documented ProblemDetails contract that the README and the endpoint's .Produces/.ProducesProblem OpenAPI declarations promise.

## Fix

Register a global exception handler (app.UseExceptionHandler(...) with IExceptionHandler, or a minimal fallback) mapping unexpected exceptions to a generic 500 ProblemDetails, while keeping the specific GitHubQueryException -> 503 mapping for that well-understood case.

## Resolution
Added builder.Services.AddProblemDetails() + app.UseExceptionHandler() in Program.cs so any exception not caught by the specific GitHubQueryException handler now returns a ProblemDetails 500 instead of an unhandled bare response.
title: Endpoint only catches GitHubQueryException; every other exception is unhandled
Readiness probe only checks token presence, not GitHub reachability or token validity

body:
## Problem

GetOpenPullRequestsAsync checks the cache with TryGetValue and only populates it with _cache.Set after the expensive fetch completes; there is no per-key locking or in-flight-request coalescing between the two.

## Evidence

PullRequestReportService.cs lines 38-56: TryGetValue at line 39, the expensive fetch/build at lines 44-53, _cache.Set at line 56, with no lock/semaphore around any of it.

## Impact

If N concurrent requests for the same owner arrive while the cache is cold or has just expired (multiple browser tabs, monitoring bots, or simply TTL lapsing under steady traffic), each independently misses the cache and independently triggers the full GitHub crawl -- multiplying GitHub API rate-limit consumption and backend load by the number of concurrent callers instead of serving one shared fetch.

## Fix

Serialize concurrent builds for the same cache key -- e.g. a ConcurrentDictionary<string, Lazy<Task<PullRequestReport>>> keyed per owner, or a per-key SemaphoreSlim -- so concurrent misses await one in-flight fetch instead of each re-querying GitHub.

## Resolution
Added PullRequestReportCoalescer (singleton, ConcurrentDictionary<string, Lazy<Task<PullRequestReport>>>) so concurrent cache misses for the same key share one in-flight GitHub fetch instead of each re-querying. Covered by a dedicated coalescing test.
title: Non-atomic cache check-then-set allows concurrent cache-miss stampede

body:
## Problem

GitHubOptions.Owner has a hardcoded C#-level default of "ivuorinen" (the project author's username), in addition to the same value also being set in appsettings.json.

## Evidence

Options/GitHubOptions.cs line 7: public string Owner { get; set; } = "ivuorinen"; The .Validate(options => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(options.Owner), ...) check in Program.cs line 18 can never fail because of this default, unless someone explicitly sets GitHub__Owner="".

## Impact

Anyone who forks/redeploys this service and forgets to set GitHub:Owner gets a service that starts, passes readiness, and returns HTTP 200 -- but silently reports pull requests for ivuorinen's repositories instead of failing loudly or reporting on the deployer's own account. The "required" validation exists but is defeated by the default.

## Fix

Remove the hardcoded fallback (default to string.Empty or leave unset) so a missing GitHub:Owner genuinely fails the !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace validation (once paired with .ValidateOnStart()) instead of silently substituting the author's account.

## Resolution
GitHubOptions.Owner default changed from "ivuorinen" to string.Empty; a missing GitHub:Owner now genuinely fails the existing required-field validation (paired with .ValidateOnStart()) instead of silently substituting the author's account.
title: GitHubOptions.Owner defaults to the author's own GitHub username

body:
## Problem

The runtime stage doesn't declare USER app (or USER $APP_UID). Per Microsoft's own documentation, .NET 8+ base images make the non-root "app" user available but do not enable it by default for standard (non-chiseled) aspnet images -- it must be opted into explicitly with a USER instruction.

## Evidence

Dockerfile lines 14-19:
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0 AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
ENV ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080
EXPOSE 8080
COPY --from=build /app/publish .
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "GhPrApi.dll"]
No USER line. Confirmed via Microsoft Learn ("Introduction to .NET and Docker" / "Users" section): "Starting with .NET 8, all images include a non-root user called app. By default, chiseled images are configured with this user enabled... In all other scenarios, the app user can be set manually, for example with the USER Dockerfile instruction."

## Impact

The container runs the ASP.NET Core process as root inside the container, unnecessarily widening the blast radius of any future code-execution vulnerability (container escape, arbitrary file write inside the image) compared to running as the provided unprivileged app user.

## Fix

Add USER app (or USER $APP_UID) to the runtime stage, after WORKDIR /app and before ENTRYPOINT.

## Resolution
Added `USER app` to the Dockerfile runtime stage. Verified: `docker run --entrypoint id` on the built image reports uid=1654(app), confirming non-root.
title: Runtime container has no explicit non-root USER, so it runs as root

body:
## Problem

The nested pullRequests(first: $prLimit, ...) GraphQL connection requests no pageInfo, so any repository with more open PRs than PullRequestLimitPerRepository (default 100) silently drops the rest; the outer pagination loop in GetOpenPullRequestsAsync also stops once RepositoryLimit is reached even if hasNextPage is still true. Neither case is surfaced anywhere in the response.

## Evidence

GitHubGraphQlClient.cs lines 32-59: the pullRequests(first: $prLimit, ...) field has no pageInfo block, unlike the outer repositories(...) connection which does (lines 22-25). Lines 137-171: the loop exits on repositoriesRead < repositoryLimit with no flag recorded when it stops early. PullRequestReport (Models/PullRequestReport.cs lines 5-10) has no truncated/hasMore field.

## Impact

The service's stated purpose is to list "currently open pull requests," but for any repo with >100 open PRs, or any owner with more repos than RepositoryLimit allows scanning, the response silently under-reports -- totalCount reflects only what was fetched, and nothing tells the consumer the dashboard is incomplete.

## Fix

Request pageInfo { hasNextPage } on the nested pullRequests connection too, and add a truncated/hasMore boolean to PullRequestReport set when either limit is hit, so downstream consumers can detect an incomplete result.

## Resolution
Added pageInfo{hasNextPage} to the nested pullRequests GraphQL connection; threaded a Truncated flag through GitHubOpenPullRequestsResult -> PullRequestReportBuilder.Build -> PullRequestReport.Truncated (set when either the per-repo PR limit or the RepositoryLimit cuts results short). README JSON example and field docs updated. Covered by new GitHubGraphQlClientTests truncation cases and a PullRequestReportBuilder passthrough test.
title: Per-repository and total-repository result limits truncate silently

body:
## Problem

Every pure-function normalizer/detector has a dedicated test file, but GitHubGraphQlClient (pagination loop, GraphQL error mapping, token/auth handling) and PullRequestReportService (cache hit/miss/refresh, enrichment orchestration) have none. Additionally, FixedTimeProvider and CreateBuilder are duplicated verbatim across two test files instead of shared.

## Evidence

tests/GhPrApi.Tests/ file listing: BranchNormalizerTests.cs, CiNormalizerTests.cs, DependencyNameDetectorTests.cs, MarkdownReportFormatterTests.cs, PullRequestReportBuilderTests.cs, ReviewNormalizerTests.cs, RobotDetectorTests.cs, SecurityDetectorTests.cs, TestPullRequests.cs -- no GitHubGraphQlClientTests.cs or PullRequestReportServiceTests.cs. The identical private FixedTimeProvider class and CreateBuilder factory appear at MarkdownReportFormatterTests.cs lines 64-83 and again at PullRequestReportBuilderTests.cs lines 110-129.

## Impact

The classes carrying the actual pagination logic, the silent-truncation bug, the N+1 pattern, the cache-stampede gap, and GraphQL error-to-exception mapping (all filed separately in this audit) are exactly the classes with no regression protection -- precisely where such bugs go undetected by dotnet test in CI.

## Fix

Add tests for PullRequestReportService using a fake IGitHubGraphQlClient (cache-hit short-circuit, cache-miss populates cache, refresh=true bypasses cache) and for GitHubGraphQlClient using a fake HttpMessageHandler (multi-page pagination, non-success HTTP status, GraphQL errors array). Extract the duplicated FixedTimeProvider/CreateBuilder helpers into one shared internal test fixture.

## Resolution
Added GitHubGraphQlClientTests.cs (pagination stitching, both truncation paths, non-success HTTP and GraphQL-error exception mapping, health-state recovery) and PullRequestReportServiceTests.cs (cache hit/miss/refresh-bypass, coalescing, per-PR status enrichment). Extracted duplicated FixedTimeProvider/CreateBuilder into shared TestSupport.cs. Suite grew from 8 files/~30 tests to 11 files/48 tests, all passing.
title: GitHubGraphQlClient and PullRequestReportService -- the most integration-heavy classes -- have zero test coverage

body:
## Problem

The repository has no LICENSE/LICENSE.md file anywhere.

## Evidence

Repository root listing (ls -la) shows: .dockerignore, .editorconfig, .env.example, .git, .github, .gitignore, compose.yml, Directory.Build.props, Dockerfile, gh-pr-api.slnx, global.json, README.md, src, tests -- no license file present, and README.md contains no license section.

## Impact

This project is documented as being published to a public GHCR image (ghcr.io/ivuorinen/gh-pr-api) and, implicitly, a public GitHub repository. Without an explicit license, copyright law defaults to "all rights reserved" -- no one may legally copy, modify, or redistribute the code even though it's publicly visible, undermining any expectation of reuse for a publicly-published image.

## Fix

Add a LICENSE file with the intended license (e.g. MIT, matching the permissive licenses of the project's own dependencies) at the repository root.

## Resolution
Added an MIT LICENSE file at the repository root.
title: No LICENSE file in the repository

body:
## Problem

Every uses: step in both workflows references a floating major-version tag (@v4, @v3, @v5, @v6) rather than a pinned full commit SHA.

## Evidence

ci.yml lines 17, 20 (actions/checkout@v4, actions/setup-dotnet@v4); container.yml lines 20, 23, 26, 34, 44 (actions/checkout@v4, docker/setup-buildx-action@v3, docker/login-action@v3, docker/metadata-action@v5, docker/build-push-action@v6).

## Impact

A version tag can be moved to point at a different commit (compromised maintainer account or upstream repo compromise), silently changing what code runs in CI. Impact is amplified in container.yml, which holds packages: write and pushes images to GHCR (lines 11-13, 43-53) -- a compromised action version there could push a malicious image under this project's identity.

## Fix

Pin each uses: to a full commit SHA (with a # vX.Y.Z comment for readability), per GitHub's action-hardening guidance; keep pins current via Dependabot's github-actions ecosystem.

## Resolution
Pinned every action in ci.yml and container.yml to its currently-referenced tag's verified commit SHA (via git ls-remote), each with a `# vX` comment. Added .github/dependabot.yml (github-actions + docker + nuget ecosystems, weekly) to keep pins current.
title: All GitHub Actions are pinned to mutable version tags, not commit SHAs

body:
## Problem

Directory.Build.props at the repository root applies to both src/GhPrApi and tests/GhPrApi.Tests (MSBuild auto-imports it into every project below it; there is no project-specific override). It sets LangVersion=preview and suppresses CA1707 (identifiers should not contain underscores) globally, even though the underscore convention this exists for (test method names like Normalize_maps_branch_status) is a test-only pattern.

## Evidence

Directory.Build.props lines 1-11: <LangVersion>preview</LangVersion>, <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>, <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);CA1707</NoWarn>. No tests/Directory.Build.props exists to scope these to the test project. global.json pins the SDK to 10.0.100 with "rollForward": "latestFeature", allowing the SDK to move to a later feature band.

## Impact

LangVersion=preview opts the production API code into non-final, potentially-changing C# language features, combined with TreatWarningsAsErrors=true -- a feature-band SDK update (permitted by rollForward: latestFeature) that changes preview-feature behavior or adds a new preview-related warning could break the build without any source change. The global CA1707 suppression also silences a real naming-convention analyzer for production code where it was never meant to apply.

## Fix

Scope LangVersion=preview and the CA1707 suppression to the test project only (e.g. via tests/Directory.Build.props), leaving src/GhPrApi on a stable, released LangVersion and with CA1707 enforced.

## Resolution
Removed LangVersion=preview from Directory.Build.props entirely (no preview-only syntax was actually in use). Moved the CA1707 (underscore-identifier) suppression into a new tests/Directory.Build.props, scoped to the test project only; src/ now has CA1707 enforced. Note: the nested Directory.Build.props initially shadowed the root one (MSBuild default behavior) -- fixed by chain-importing the parent via GetPathOfFileAbove, verified by a clean dotnet build.
title: Preview C# language version and a naming-rule suppression apply to production code, not just tests

body:
## Problem

Both Dockerfile stages reference mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/{sdk,aspnet}:10.0 -- a floating tag that moves to newer patch builds over time -- rather than a specific patch version or digest. Separately, .dockerignore excludes bin/, obj/, and VCS/IDE cruft, but not tests/ or README.md, so the full test-source tree is sent to the Docker daemon on every build even though the Dockerfile's COPY instructions never reference it.

## Evidence

Dockerfile lines 3, 14 (FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0 AS build, FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0 AS runtime). .dockerignore full contents: .git, .github, bin, obj, **/bin, **/obj, TestResults, **/TestResults, .vs, .vscode, .idea, *.user, *.suo, .env, .env.*, !/.env.example -- no tests/ or README.md entry.

## Impact

A floating tag means two docker build runs on different days/machines can produce images built on different underlying 10.0.x patch releases without any Dockerfile change -- not fully reproducible. The unfiltered build context uploads the entire tests/ tree to the daemon on every build for no benefit.

## Fix

Pin the base images to a specific patch tag or digest (e.g. mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0.x@sha256:...) and add tests/ and README.md to .dockerignore.

## Resolution
Pinned both Dockerfile base images (sdk:10.0, aspnet:10.0) to their current registry digests, verified via `docker buildx imagetools inspect`. Added tests/ and README.md to .dockerignore. Verified with a full `docker build` (succeeded).
title: Base images pinned only to a floating minor tag; build context includes unneeded source
Full HTTP response body is logged verbatim and unbounded on any non-success GitHub response

body:
## Problem

Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi 10.0.0 transitively pulls Microsoft.OpenApi 2.0.0, which NuGet's audit feature flags via GHSA-v5pm-xwqc-g5wc (CVE-2026-49451, high severity, stack-overflow DoS on circular schema refs). Because Directory.Build.props sets TreatWarningsAsErrors=true, this NuGet audit warning (NU1903) is escalated to a build-breaking error on src/GhPrApi.csproj. This was not caught during the initial review because no `dotnet build`/`dotnet restore` was run as part of that pass -- only static code reading.

## Evidence

Running `dotnet restore` (and `dotnet build`) on the untouched repository fails with:
/Users/ivuorinen/Code/ivuorinen/gh-pr-api/src/GhPrApi/GhPrApi.csproj : error NU1903: Warning As Error: Package 'Microsoft.OpenApi' 2.0.0 has a known high severity vulnerability, https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v5pm-xwqc-g5wc
Build FAILED.

## Impact

The project cannot be restored or built at all in its committed state -- `dotnet restore`, `dotnet build`, `dotnet test`, the Dockerfile's `dotnet restore`/`dotnet publish` steps, and ci.yml's Restore/Build/Test steps all fail identically. This is a total build outage, not a latent risk: every CI run and every local `dotnet build` fails before a single line of application code executes.

## Fix

Add a direct PackageReference to Microsoft.OpenApi pinned to the patched version (2.7.5, per the advisory's remediation) in src/GhPrApi/GhPrApi.csproj, overriding the vulnerable transitive version pulled in by Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi 10.0.0.

## Resolution
Added a direct PackageReference to Microsoft.OpenApi 2.7.5 (the patched version per GHSA-v5pm-xwqc-g5wc) in src/GhPrApi/GhPrApi.csproj, overriding the vulnerable transitive 2.0.0 pulled in by Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi 10.0.0. Verified: dotnet restore/build now succeed with 0 warnings/0 errors.
title: Project fails to restore/build at all: NU1903 security-advisory warning escalated to a hard error

body:
## Problem

The nested labels(first: 50) clause, combined with the already-max repoPageSize (100) and prLimit (100) that the app's own default configuration produces, made every request to the GraphQL API request 510,100 possible nodes -- over GitHub's hard 500,000-node ceiling. This was not a rare edge case: it reproduced on the very first real call once a valid token was configured, using nothing but the values already committed in appsettings.json.

## Evidence

Reported at runtime: "GitHub GraphQL returned 1 errors. First error: This query requests up to 510,100 possible nodes which exceeds the maximum limit of 500,000." Node math: 100 (repos) + 100*100 (PRs) + 100*100*50 (labels) = 510,100, matching the error exactly.

## Impact

The /api/github/open-pull-requests endpoint was completely non-functional out of the box -- every call failed with 503 "Unable to query GitHub." regardless of token validity, since the underlying GraphQL query itself was rejected by GitHub before any data could be returned.

## Fix

Reduced labels(first: 50) to labels(first: 20), bringing the worst-case node count to 210,100 (safely under the limit even at max page sizes). Added a regression test (GitHubGraphQlClientTests) that extracts the live query via reflection and asserts the worst-case node count stays under 500,000, so a future limit increase gets caught at test time.

## Resolution
Reduced labels(first: 50) to labels(first: 20) in OpenPullRequestsQuery; added a reflection-based regression test asserting the worst-case node count stays under GitHub's 500,000 limit.
title: OpenPullRequestsQuery exceeds GitHub's 500,000-node GraphQL limit with the shipped default config

body:
## Problem

The GitHub HttpClient had no resilience policy: a single transient failure (5xx, timeout, connection reset) from GitHub's own infrastructure failed the entire request immediately, surfacing as 503 to the caller with no retry.

## Evidence

Observed in production use: a request to https://api.github.com/graphql returned HTTP 502 (nginx) after 10.75s, logged via GitHubGraphQlClient's warning and surfaced as 503 "Unable to query GitHub." with no retry attempted.

## Impact

Any transient blip on GitHub's side -- which are common for third-party API consumers -- fails the user-facing request outright instead of self-healing, even though a retry would likely have succeeded.

## Fix

Added Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience's AddStandardResilienceHandler() to the GitHub HttpClient registration (retry with exponential backoff + jitter on 5xx/408/timeouts, circuit breaker, bounded total-request timeout). Tuned AttemptTimeout to 15s (default 10s was too tight given observed real GitHub latency), CircuitBreaker.SamplingDuration to 30s, and TotalRequestTimeout to 70s. Verified: app starts cleanly with the new options (no startup validation failure) and dotnet build/test remain clean.

## Resolution
Added Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience's AddStandardResilienceHandler() to the GitHub HttpClient with tuned AttemptTimeout/CircuitBreaker/TotalRequestTimeout. Verified clean startup and dotnet build/test.
title: No retry/backoff on transient GitHub API failures

body:
## Problem

Even after fixing the static 500,000-node ceiling violation, a repoPageSize of 100 (paired with prLimit=100, labels=20 -> 210,100 nodes) was still too expensive for GitHub's GraphQL backend to execute within its own timeout budget. This is a distinct problem from the node-count ceiling: GitHub's edge (nginx) times out waiting on its backend and returns 502 before the static validation-error path is even reached.

## Evidence

Observed in production use: 4 consecutive attempts (initial + 3 retries via the newly-added resilience handler) each took ~10.5-11s and each returned HTTP 502 from nginx -- consistent timing across every attempt, not the random variance expected from transient infrastructure flakiness. Total elapsed 52.6s across all 4 attempts, all failing identically.

## Impact

Retries cannot fix a deterministically-too-expensive query -- the endpoint was still completely non-functional for this workload even with the earlier node-limit and resilience fixes in place, just failing more slowly (52s instead of instantly).

## Fix

Reduced the repository page size cap from 100 to 10 (new MaxRepositoryPageSize constant), cutting worst-case per-request node count from 210,100 to 21,010. RepositoryLimit's overall semantics are unchanged -- the existing cursor-pagination loop simply now fetches more, smaller pages instead of fewer, heavier ones. Updated the existing node-count regression test to read the real page-size cap via reflection instead of a hardcoded assumption, so it can't go stale again.

## Resolution
Reduced repository page size cap from 100 to 10 (MaxRepositoryPageSize constant) in GitHubGraphQlClient; updated the node-count regression test to read the real cap via reflection.
title: Repository page size (100) makes OpenPullRequestsQuery too expensive for GitHub to execute, causing consistent 502s
